definition: Total value of all invoiced sales before returns, discounts and VAT.
Gross revenue minus returns, discounts and VAT. This is the revenue figure used in management reporting.
(Net revenue - cost of goods sold) / net revenue, shown as a percentage. Measures how much of each euro of revenue is left after direct costs.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Used as a proxy for operating cash profitability.
Average number of days it takes to collect payment after an invoice is issued. Calculated as accounts receivable / net revenue x days in period.
A customer with at least one paid order in the last 90 days.
Net revenue divided by the number of paid orders in the same period.
A previously active customer with no paid order for more than 180 days.
Total marketing and sales spend in a period divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period.
Share of website sessions that end in a paid order, shown as a percentage.
Time since the last successful pipeline run. Dashboards show a "stale" warning if it exceeds 24 hours.
German term for revenue — tests that ä, ö, ü and ß survive the trip to Snowflake and Metabase.
Has no owner field, to check optional columns stay empty instead of breaking the load.
Recurring costs to run the business, such as salaries, rent and software, excluding cost of goods sold.
Spending on long-term assets such as equipment or buildings that are capitalised and depreciated over time.
Direct costs of producing or purchasing the goods sold in a period, including materials and direct labour.
Profit after all expenses, interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation have been deducted from revenue.
Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. Shows the cash available after maintaining and growing the asset base.
Money customers owe for goods or services already invoiced but not yet paid.
Money the company owes to suppliers for goods or services received but not yet paid.
Difference between actual and budgeted figures for a period. A positive variance on revenue or a negative variance on cost is favourable.
Net cash spent per month when expenses exceed income. Used to estimate how long current cash will last.
Current assets minus current liabilities. Indicates whether the company can cover its short-term obligations.
Sum of normalised monthly subscription revenue from all active contracts at the end of a month.
Monthly recurring revenue multiplied by twelve. Used to express the annual value of subscription contracts.
Expected total net revenue from a customer over the whole relationship, based on average order value, purchase frequency and retention.
Share of closed sales opportunities that were won, shown as a percentage of all closed opportunities in the period.
Total expected value of all open sales opportunities, before weighting by probability to close.
Average number of days from opportunity creation to a won deal.
A customer whose first paid order falls within the reporting period.
Share of customers with two or more paid orders in the period, out of all customers with at least one paid order.
Recurring revenue from existing customers at the end of a period, including upsell and minus churn, divided by their recurring revenue at the start.
Total discounts granted divided by gross revenue before discounts, shown as a percentage.
Clicks divided by impressions for an ad or email, shown as a percentage.
Ad spend divided by the number of clicks the ads received.
Marketing spend divided by the number of new leads generated in the same period.
Net revenue attributed to advertising divided by ad spend. A ROAS of 4 means 4 euros of revenue per euro spent.
A lead whose engagement meets the agreed scoring threshold and is ready to be passed to sales.
A marketing qualified lead that sales has reviewed and accepted as a real opportunity.
Share of leads created in a period that became paying customers, shown as a percentage.
Unique email opens divided by delivered emails, shown as a percentage. Affected by privacy features that pre-load images.
Share of website sessions with only one page view and no interaction, shown as a percentage.
Number of days after an ad click or view during which a conversion is credited to that ad. Our default is 30 days after click.
Average hours from order payment to shipment handover to the carrier.
Share of orders delivered on or before the promised delivery date, shown as a percentage.
Number of returned order lines divided by shipped order lines in the same period, shown as a percentage.
Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory value. Shows how many times stock is sold and replaced in a period.
Share of active products with zero available stock at the end of the day, shown as a percentage.
An order line that was accepted but cannot be shipped because the product is out of stock.
Days between placing a purchase order with a supplier and receiving the goods in the warehouse.
Share of customer support tickets solved in the first interaction without follow-up, shown as a percentage.
Average minutes a support agent spends on one ticket, including conversation and follow-up work.
Percentage of promoters (score 9–10) minus percentage of detractors (score 0–6) from the customer survey. Ranges from -100 to 100.
The single system or table agreed as authoritative for a given metric or entity. Reports must use it over copies.
A table that records business events, such as orders or payments, with numeric measures and keys to dimensions. Prefixed fct_.
A table that describes business entities, such as customers or products, used to filter and group facts. Prefixed dim_.
A dbt model that cleans and renames one source table without business logic. Prefixed stg_ and not meant for reporting.
What one row of a table represents, for example one order line per day. Always check the grain before joining or summing.
A generated unique identifier for a row, used instead of business keys that may change or collide across sources.
A dimension that keeps history of changing attributes, such as a customer's segment, with valid-from and valid-to dates.
The path data takes from source systems through transformations to reports, showing which models depend on which.
Shared business definitions of metrics, dimensions and terms that sit between raw data and reports so everyone calculates numbers the same way.
An automated check, such as unique or not null, that runs after each build and fails the pipeline if data breaks an agreed rule.
